annotation.reasoning_summary: The dataset represents specific housing blocks owned by housing associations, treated as individual objects or real-world assets. Topology hints (low shared_boundary_ratio, low convex_hull_fill_ratio) confirm these are discrete features rather than a full-area tessellation. ObjectDS is chosen because the polygons represent identifiable real-world managed assets.

The layer maps specific archaeological sites, such as cesspits and find spots, represented as points. These are discrete real-world archaeological objects or locations, fitting the ObjectDS definition.
The dataset maps specific archaeological find locations as point features, where each point represents an identifiable archaeological object or asset, fitting the definition of ObjectDS.

The dataset contains polygons representing specific archeological sites, which are distinct, identifiable, real-world bounded objects or locations of historical interest. These do not form a complete coverage or tessellation of the city, and the topology hints (low shared boundary ratio, low fill ratios) support classifying them as discrete objects rather than reporting units or coverage classes.
The map displays specific areas (parks/zones) where barbecue rules apply, which are isolated polygons rather than a complete partition or reporting units. Therefore, it is a PatchDS.

The dataset maps specific protected urban and village areas (conservation areas), which function as discrete, named real-world objects rather than exhaustive reporting units or categorical coverage. The low shared_boundary_ratio and isolated nature of the polygons confirm the PlainVectorRegion geometry classification.

The layer represents point-based biological observations (wild bees) conducted at specific locations over different years. These are field surveys/inventories of species presence at discrete locations, which best fits the EventDS entity category.

The layer represents locations of honey bee hives (bee colonies), which are discrete real-world objects. While numeric attributes exist (number of hives), they describe the properties of the objects rather than making the layer an AmountDS.

The dataset represents a comprehensive, area-wide thematic classification of soil quality in Amsterdam, partitioning the city into various zones. The high shared_boundary_ratio and adjacency confirm a tessellation geometry, and the categorical nature of the soil quality attributes across the entire study area qualifies it as a CoverageDS.
The dataset maps individual trees as point features. These are distinct, countable real-world assets managed by the municipality, fitting the definition of an ObjectDS.

The dataset contains point locations representing individual trees, which are clearly discrete, real-world objects. The numeric attributes (e.g., boomnummer, plantjaar) are characteristics of these objects, not the primary mapped phenomenon.

The map displays point locations of neighborhood compost initiatives, which represent distinct real-world facilities or projects.

The layer represents individual trees, each identified by a unique ID (Boomnummer) and spatial point location, making it an ObjectDS. Although there are attributes related to maintenance and timing, these describe the objects rather than representing them as events or statistical amounts.

While the area size attribute is numeric, the points function as identifiers for the infestations rather than a purely numeric data map.
